title: The Warm Wall
blurb: The Chapterhouse wall is warm, every stand pair is wrong, and the floor has something to say.

blocks.text: Braziers crackle somewhere behind me. My palm is flat on the Chapterhouse wall.
The wall is warm.

Cellar slowstone is never warm. You could keep milk against it in August. Someone has opened the great doors to the braziered hall upstairs and let the city's heat roll down the steps, and every stand pair I worked out from this floor chart last night, by candle, with string, is wrong before I've set a foot on it.
The Warden swings his tell-weight once. "Pace six."
Legal. Fast. Nobody blinks but me.
I turn to tell Marten, and stop, and turn again. Properly this time. Square, feet to his feet, my face in the lamplight, the way you'd set a stone to its bed.
He's already looking at my mouth. Of course he is. He has been all season.
"Pace six," I say.
"Aye. Saw him say it."

Nine rounds. Every joke I've cracked out of the side of my face, every "good draw" I've thrown over my shoulder on a stair, has gone past him like rain past a window. What he got was the count. Three. Two. Draw. I gave him that one facing him, mouth wide, because I thought he needed the timing spelled out. He needed it spelled out because it was the only thing I ever said where he could see it.
And I'm the one who turns my left side to people and says "other side" so nobody asks. Two Dampers in one beam, each doing the other's trick backwards. You'd think one of us would have noticed.
"How long?" I say.
"Since before you."
"You never said."
"You never asked facing me." He nods at the floor: nineteen stands, twelve plates going amber in the lamplight. "Tonight you ask facing me. Every throw."
"Every throw. And you wait for it."
"Aye, well. I always have."
That's true. In Round 4 he drew on time. I was the one who came in late, checking him.

There's no checking tonight. Marten is on thirty-nine. If he draws a tenth of a count before me, the note goes into him whole, the Mark goes into the Book, and the Chapter Rings him Out on its own floor on his last night.
Quist walked us as far as the Chapterhouse steps and no further. He's out there now in the cold, boots on.

At the floor's edge stands a man in Chapter grey with a white band at his throat, hands folded over a brass rod as long as a walking stick. Soft face. Kind eyes. He watches us strip our boots as if we were his nephews home for the holiday.
"Precentor Thale," Sef says, on my right. "Head of the whole Chapter. Came down special."
Sef goes to the Warden about the doors. The Warden looks past him. It's Thale who answers, soft as a sermon.
"The hall is open to the city on promotion night, Mr Brask. It always has been. People should see the good of the game, and they shouldn't freeze to see it." He smiles. "Our city is cold enough."
"Custom," Sef says.
"Most things here are."
So I kneel on the floor with the chart spread out under my palms and start again.

At pace six, sound walks a fifth faster than it did at home. Every wave stretches by a fifth. A pair that killed a note at Kilnyard now kills one about three semitones higher; the whole band slides up the scale like a wedge driven under a stone. And the bottom falls off. Five paces is still the longest wave any pair can take, but at six, a five-pace wave is a note that would have been barely over four at home. Everything lower walks straight through us.
"Say them," Sef says, crouching on my right, pencil going.
I say them. "Nine and fourteen, one-point-nine along the straight path from their left Calling stand. Eleven and the Last Stand, one-point-six. Twelve and the Last Stand, two-point-two."
He says each one back to me, word for word, while his pencil scratches loops in the notebook. He never looks down at it. I've stopped pretending not to see that.

"Seventeen pairs," he says. "Three things. One, the Last Stand pairs are the only ones left for anything middling. Two, everything their big lad throws is too long now. Three, no, four, the doors stay open, so it gets worse."
"It gets worse," Oduya agrees.

She's at the plate rail. She found it in the half-dark without looking for it, the way you find your own kitchen drawer at night. Her palm rests on our Last Plate, and for a moment she doesn't move at all.
"Heat in a Drum is heat under a pan, Wren Halloway," she says, without turning round. "It doesn't announce itself. It just keeps coming."
Thale watches us kindly from the edge, his rod's brass foot resting on the stone beside his shoe, the way an old man rests a stick.
I walk to the Last Stand.

I've never played it. In Round 8 I stood on one for a single throw with my hands at my sides. This one sits under our Last Plate with the wall a pace behind my heels. I tap it with my heel. It rings true, deep and clean, deeper than a stand has any right to. The Warden sees me tap it and lets it go.

The Cantors' Lads sing in the Chapter choir on feast days and play the Cellar Ring the rest of the year. Sef has named them already. Their Scribe is the Sexton, thin and tidy. Their Callers are Candle, high and narrow, and Bellows, chest like a cask.

First throw. Candle's lead-in comes up through my soles before its glow has crawled a pace. I know the pitch. I turn my face to Marten and shape the stand: "Eleven." He steps. The Raise ends. I keep my face on him.
"Three. Two. Draw."
We draw. The note dies between us. Under my feet, something small and whole goes down through the stand like a pebble dropped in a well. I don't wait to feel where it lands.
"Nothing, Halloway. Nothing, Sallow."
The gallery murmurs. Ghost quell, someone says. On their floor, against their own lads.

By the fourth throw the heat has crept further in. I reach back between throws and lay a palm on the wall behind me: warmer than the last time. Faster pace, longer waves. Candle's next pitch reads clean through my feet, and the pair I'd have picked for it is out of band by a hair, a doubling dressed up as a null.
I face Marten. "Off."
He nods. Neither of us draws. The note shoves through both of us, loses two weight, and still has enough to ring our plate. First Peal to the Lads.

Dov answers with the Mordant and names it to the gallery. One-one. Bellows throws long and low, too long for anything we've got, and we body-block it, and Oduya's peg sends it rattling a semitone and a half wide. Candle throws again and I call the pair off again, and that one Peals.
Two-one to the Lads at the Half. Marten has not drawn once without my mouth telling him to. Not early. Not once.
The Long Ground. Nobody's holding anything to clear. I spend it with my back to the wall, palm flat, learning the heat.
Marten Grounds anyway, with nothing in him to Ground, humming the lullaby down into his stand. I step round to his front.
"It'll be faster after the Half," I say. "The walls are still climbing."
"Then you'll know before he says it." He tips his head at the Warden. "And I'll know when you do."
"Pace six and a half," the Warden says.

The second Half is a dogfight. Bellows opens with a long one, seven paces if it's a hair, too long for any pair on any floor. It shoves through Marten, then through me, and knocks me clean off the Last Stand. I step straight back on. I can't draw until the next throw, but there was nothing to draw it with anyway. It Peals, and we're two behind. Dov Peals the Widowmaker. Then the Ferret, which he only throws when he's frightened, because it goes in sideways and nobody expects it. Three-three.
Four throws left for them. Four for us.
The Sexton has been doing what Sef does. Their Scribe can count Marks as well as anyone. He tips his head to his Callers, and from then on everything they have comes at the Last Stand.

Of course it does. Marten is on thirty-nine. Every note into our pair is a chance for a doubling, and a doubling is a Mark, and the next Mark is forty. It's legal. Marten isn't lit. It's just good Scribing, with a man on the end of it.

They throw warm, every one. Oduya is walking our peg a semitone a Breath, and a cold throw drifting two semitones would rattle off it for nothing. So they hum their lead-ins, and the lead-ins come up through my feet, and I read every one.
Candle. Weight four. The pitch comes up through the stand as clear as a struck chisel.
I don't look at the note. I look at Marten. "Eleven."
He steps.
"Three. Two. Draw."
It dies. Down it goes, into the stone.
"Nothing, Halloway. Nothing, Sallow."

Bellows next, straining up to chase Oduya's peg, his voice going reedy at the top. That's two semitones higher than his comfort and it shortens his wave into reach. I feel it come and I'm already turned. "Twelve." Marten steps. I give him the count and I don't check him. I don't check him. We draw, and the air goes flat and still between us.
"Nothing, Halloway. Nothing, Sallow."
Our throw. Dov looks at Marten across the floor, and for once he doesn't play to the gallery.
"This one's the Long Goodnight," he says. "For him."
He voices it low and kind and dead on their peg. Their Last Plate rings. One. Two. Three.
Four-three.

Candle again. She's frightened now and it shows in her lead-in, which wobbles before it settles. I take it from the floor when it settles. "Eleven." The heat has nudged the band since last time. I can feel the edge of it, the way you feel a joint that's nearly true. Nearly is a doubling. I put my palm to the wall behind me, once, and the warmth tells me it's still inside.
"Three. Two. Draw."
Dead.
Last throw of the match. Bellows. Weight five, all he's got left, pitched high again to chase the peg, the lead-in like a cart rolling over a cellar door.
If this one gets through and Peals, it's four-four and a Sudden Peal. If our pair is off by a tenth of a pace, it's a doubling, and Marten is Rung Out on the last throw of his life.
I feel the pitch. I know the pair.
I turn my face to Marten. His eyes are on my mouth, steady, patient, a working dad's eyes waiting for a slow child to finish a sentence.
"Twelve."
He steps. The Raise ends. The glow comes crawling at us across the Drum, wide and dull, and I never look at it.
"Three. Two. Draw."
We draw in the same instant. I know because there's nothing. No shove, no ring, no buzz in the bones. The front of the glow simply isn't there any more.
"Nothing, Halloway. Nothing, Sallow."
The match is over.
Nobody moves for a moment. The gallery is drawing breath to shout. In that hush, standing barefoot on the Last Stand with no ring in me at all, I feel the floor answer.
Four notes come up through the stand. They're the four I just killed, in the order I killed them, pitch for pitch, as clear as if someone had tapped them out on a banker under my feet.
Then one more. A fifth. New.
Then a held silence, the kind that's waiting for something.
It isn't an echo. Echoes don't add.
The gallery breaks. Dov is shouting. Jory is jumping on the stair. Sef has both hands on his head. The Warden is writing. Nobody in this Drum has felt a thing except me.
Thale is still at the floor's edge, both hands folded on his rod, its foot on the stone. He is looking at me. He is smiling.
Marten steps off his stand. He doesn't hurry. He walks to the Warden and waits until the man's mouth has finished moving.
"Thirty-nine, Sallow," the Warden says. "Retiring?"
"Aye," Marten says. "On my feet."
He walks off the floor humming the lullaby, and the gallery, who have no idea what they're clapping, clap him all the way up the steps.
The antechamber has a stone floor and a clerk with a strongbox. Kilnyard finish second, seven wins and two losses. The Tannery Hounds are champions. We go up to the Vault League.
The clerk counts twenty crowns into Sef's hands. Sef holds them for a second as if they might fly off. Then he turns and puts every one of them into mine.
"One," he says, "it's yours. Two, don't argue. Three, we voted on the cart."
"I proposed it," Dov says, "so technically it's my idea. You're welcome."
"Aye," Marten says.
"You will take it, Wren Halloway," Oduya says, very quietly, which is worse than any shout.
Twenty, and the six in my tin. Twenty-six. It's the most money I've held in my life, and it's still twelve short.
The Guild bailiff is waiting by the hall door in his good coat. He's come for the lot tonight; it's Quarter Day tomorrow. He looks at the coins, and at the side, and at me.
"Your master's debt, Halloway," he says.
I don't correct him. I never do. Everyone in this room just handed me their purse for a dead man's debt, and I let them, and that sits in me like a cracked lintel nobody else can see.
"Anybody want a doorstep?" I say. "I'll do you a cheap one. Who's carrying this home? Twenty crowns in a coat is a mugging."
The bailiff doesn't laugh. He takes out the bond and reads it again.
"The Guild extends once," he says, "to Lady Day, for a member whose side has promoted. Never twice." He writes it in the margin and signs it. "Lady Day, Halloway. Twelve crowns."
Then he's gone, and I'm standing barefoot on cold stone with a fistful of money and three more months.

Sef is on my right, where he always is now. I take his wrist without explaining and tap it out on the inside of it with two fingers. The floor's reply. Long, short, short, long, and the fifth one, last and alone.
He goes still.

Sef is never still. He is the noisiest thinker in Caddrow. He stands there with his wrist in my hand and says nothing at all, and then he reaches past me and taps the same five on the doorframe, faster, surer, the way he tapped every notch of the lintel the morning after it was chiselled away.
"That's the end of the lintel," he says. "The last notches. In order."
My boots are still on the bench in the Drum.

I go back down for them alone. The braziers are burning low. Somebody has finally shut the great doors, and the cold is already creeping back into the walls; I can feel it through my soles on the steps.
The Drum is empty. Not quite.
Precentor Thale is kneeling on the Last Stand. My stand. His eyes are shut, and the brass foot of his listening rod is pressed hard to the stone.

He doesn't startle when I come in. He lifts the rod, gets up slowly, the way old knees do, and walks across the floor to me. He stops on my right side, where I can hear him, as if somebody had told him.
"Who taught you to say that?" he asks quietly.
